headline: Trump went to Michigan to call El-Sayed a jihadist.
summary: President Trump told a crowd in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday that he was there to keep "a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member" out of the Senate. He meant Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee, who would be the first Muslim senator. El-Sayed has disavowed the Brotherhood and says he is loyal to the US. The vote is November 3.
cover_answer: It shouldn't. The Constitution lets everyone pray their way.
table_question: Should how someone prays ever count against them for a job?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The president went to Michigan and said a man who wants a job in the Senate is dangerous because of how he prays. The man, Abdul El-Sayed, is Muslim, and he says that's not true. In America you can pray any way you want, like picking any seat on the bus. Calling someone bad for their religion is wrong, and the grown-ups are on it.
5-7.why: Name-calling over religion is a playground rule they already know.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, and here that is a grown-up calling a man a bad name for how he prays, a playground rule they already own. The seat on the bus is the anchor; the Brotherhood and 9/11 stay off the card. Expect "is the man bad?" He says no, and nobody has shown otherwise. That is the answer.

8-12.script: Abdul El-Sayed is running for the Senate in Michigan. Trump says his past shows sympathy for extremists. El-Sayed says he's loyal to the US and the Constitution lets everyone pray as they choose. Like a game where one side yells "cheater" instead of playing.
8-12.why: Claim, denial, then the rule. One side yells instead of playing.
8-12.why_long: This age is checking whether adults apply the rules evenly, so the script sets the claim beside the denial and then the rule: pray as you choose. The side that shouts "cheater" instead of playing is the mechanism. Expect "so who's telling the truth?" El-Sayed has denied it every time; the AP reports no proof from Trump. Say so.

13-17.script: Would you vote against someone for how they pray? Trump told Port Huron he came to stop "a jihadist" from entering the Capitol, and likened it to the passengers of Flight 93. El-Sayed calls questioning his loyalty shameful. Why this play, now?
13-17.why: A real seat, and a pitch built on religion.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the seat is in play, and the case against the candidate is his faith. The script asks why this play, now, which the AP leaves open. Expect "would you vote for him?" Answer honestly, then ask what would change their mind. Kuhn: argument is practised, and this one is worth it.

5-7.a: He says no, and nobody has shown he is. Saying someone's bad for their religion is the wrong part.

8-12.a: It shouldn't. The Constitution guarantees the right to pray as you choose.
A movement with branches the US calls terrorist groups. He disavows it.

13-17.q: Has El-Sayed said anything wrong himself?
13-17.a: He said "hurt people hurt people" after a synagogue attack, then said sorry.
A seat is open. Republicans haven't won a Michigan Senate race in 30 years.
